entities.name: Husayn of Zaragoza
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Husayn ibn Yahya al-Ansari, known as Husayn of Zaragoza, emerged as a pivotal figure in the complex political landscape of al-Andalus during the late 8th century, serving as the Wali (governor) of Zaragoza from 774 to 781 CE. A direct descendant of Sa'd ibn Ubadah, a prominent companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Husayn leveraged his esteemed lineage and regional power base to assert a degree of autonomy against the nascent Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman I. His significance lies in his bold defiance of the centralizing Umayyad authority and, critically, his audacious alliance with the rising Carolingian power, Charlemagne, a diplomatic gamble that profoundly shaped the military and political dynamics of the Iberian Peninsula and the Frankish realm.

In 778 CE, Husayn, seeking to solidify his independence from Córdoba, extended an invitation to Charlemagne, then King of the Franks, to invade al-Andalus. This overture promised Charlemagne control over Zaragoza and other northern territories in exchange for military support against Abd al-Rahman I. Charlemagne, eager to expand his influence southward and exploit the internal divisions of al-Andalus, led a formidable Frankish army across the Pyrenees. However, upon reaching Zaragoza, Husayn, observing the overwhelming strength of the Frankish forces and perhaps wary of exchanging one overlord for another, reneged on his promise, refusing entry to Charlemagne's troops. After a month-long siege proved futile, Charlemagne was forced to withdraw, a retreat famously culminating in the devastating ambush of his rearguard at the Battle of Roncesvalles by Basque forces on August 15, 778 CE.
